title: Change in Profit-Sharing Ratio among Existing Partners
summary: When existing partners agree to share future profits in a new ratio, some partners gain and others sacrifice. This chapter explains sacrificing and gaining ratios, adjustment of goodwill, treatment of accumulated profits, reserves and losses, revaluation of assets and liabilities, and the single adjusting entry used when book values are to remain unchanged.

notes.heading: Sacrificing ratio and gaining ratio
notes.html:
A change in the profit-sharing ratio (PSR) is in effect a reconstitution of the firm: the old agreement ends and a new one begins. Some partners give up a part of their share (sacrifice) and others acquire it (gain).

  • Sacrifice of a partner = Old share − New share (positive result)
  • Gain of a partner = New share − Old share (positive result)
  • Total sacrifice always equals total gain.

Worked illustration 1

A, B and C share profits 5:3:2. From 1 April they agree to share 2:3:5.

PartnerOld shareNew shareDifferenceResult
A5/102/103/10Sacrifice
B3/103/10NilNeither
C2/105/103/10Gain

A alone sacrifices 3/10 and C alone gains 3/10.

notes.heading: Adjustment of goodwill
notes.html:
As per AS-26, goodwill is not raised in the books. The gaining partner compensates the sacrificing partner through their capital (or current) accounts for the share of goodwill gained.

SituationJournal entry
Adjustment of goodwillGaining Partner's Capital A/c Dr (goodwill x gain)
To Sacrificing Partner's Capital A/c (goodwill x sacrifice)
Goodwill already appearing in the books (write it off first, in old ratio)All Partners' Capital A/cs Dr (old ratio)
To Goodwill A/c

In illustration 1, if goodwill is valued at ₹1,00,000: C's Capital A/c Dr ₹30,000 To A's Capital A/c ₹30,000.

notes.heading: Accumulated profits, reserves and losses
notes.html:
Reserves and undistributed profits were earned while the old ratio was in force, so they belong to the partners in the old ratio. Similarly, accumulated losses are borne in the old ratio.

ItemJournal entry (old ratio)
General reserve, reserve fund, credit balance of P&LGeneral Reserve A/c Dr / Profit and Loss A/c Dr
To Partners' Capital A/cs
Debit balance of P&L, deferred revenue expenditure (e.g. advertisement suspense)Partners' Capital A/cs Dr
To Profit and Loss A/c / To Advertisement Suspense A/c

If partners want reserves to continue in the books, no distribution is made; instead a single adjusting entry is passed (see the last-but-one section).

notes.heading: Revaluation of assets and reassessment of liabilities
notes.html:
Changes in the value of assets and liabilities up to the date of change belong to partners in the old ratio. They are recorded through a Revaluation Account (a nominal account).

Dr. Revaluation Account (losses)Cr. Revaluation Account (gains)
Decrease in value of an assetIncrease in value of an asset
Increase in value of a liabilityDecrease in value of a liability
Unrecorded liability brought into booksUnrecorded asset brought into books
Profit on revaluation transferred to capitals (old ratio)Loss on revaluation transferred to capitals (old ratio)

Key entries: (i) Revaluation A/c Dr To Asset A/c (decrease); (ii) Asset A/c Dr To Revaluation A/c (increase); (iii) Revaluation A/c Dr To Partners' Capital A/cs (profit, old ratio), or the reverse for a loss.

notes.heading: Single adjusting entry when book values are not to be changed
notes.html:
If partners decide that reserves should remain and assets and liabilities should continue at old values, the net effect is adjusted between gaining and sacrificing partners by one entry:

  1. Net amount = Reserves and credit balance of P&L − Accumulated losses ± Revaluation profit/loss + Goodwill (if to be adjusted together).
  2. Gaining partner's share = Net amount x Gain; sacrificing partner's share = Net amount x Sacrifice.
  3. Entry: Gaining Partner's Capital A/c Dr To Sacrificing Partner's Capital A/c.

Worked illustration 2

Using the comprehensive illustration data: Net amount = 50,000 − 10,000 + 25,000 + 60,000 = ₹1,25,000. Y gains 1/10, so Y's Capital A/c Dr ₹12,500 To X's Capital A/c ₹12,500. Reserves, P&L balance and asset values stay as they were.

notes.heading: Common mistakes to avoid
notes.html:
• Distributing reserves or revaluation profit in the new ratio; always use the old ratio.
  • Raising goodwill in the books; under AS-26 it is adjusted only through capital accounts.
  • Forgetting to write off existing goodwill in the old ratio before adjusting the new goodwill.
  • Treating the excess of a workmen compensation claim over the reserve as a capital debit; it is a loss debited to the Revaluation Account.
  • Debiting a partner whose share is unchanged; he neither gains nor sacrifices.

keyTerms.definition: Any change in the relationship among partners, such as a change in profit-sharing ratio, admission, retirement or death.
Ratio in which partners give up their share of profit; Old ratio − New ratio.
Ratio in which partners acquire additional share of profit; New ratio − Old ratio.
Nominal account recording changes in values of assets and liabilities at the time of reconstitution; balance shared in old ratio.
Reserves and undistributed profits appearing in the balance sheet; distributed in old ratio on reconstitution.
Reserve created out of profits to meet possible claims of workers for compensation.
Reserve created to meet a possible fall in the market value of investments.
Heavy revenue expenditure (e.g. advertisement suspense) shown as an asset and written off in the old ratio on reconstitution.
Asset owned by the firm but not shown in the books; brought in by crediting the Revaluation Account.
A single entry between gaining and sacrificing partners' capital accounts that gives the net effect of reserves, losses, revaluation and goodwill without altering book values.

formulas.name: Goodwill adjustment
formulas.html: Gaining partner debited with Firm's goodwill x Gain; sacrificing partner credited with Firm's goodwill x Sacrifice

formulas.name: Net amount for single adjustment entry
formulas.html: Reserves + Credit balance of P&L − Accumulated losses ± Revaluation profit/loss (+ Goodwill, if adjusted together)

formulas.name: Share to be adjusted
formulas.html: Net amount x Gain (or Sacrifice) of the partner

mcqs.explanation: A partner sacrifices when his old share is more than his new share, so sacrifice = Old − New.

mcqs.q: A, B and C share profits 4:3:2. They decide to share 2:3:4 in future. Which partner gains and by how much?
mcqs.explanation: C: 4/9 − 2/9 = 2/9 gain; A: 4/9 − 2/9 = 2/9 sacrifice; B unchanged.

mcqs.q: In the above case, if goodwill of the firm is valued at ₹90,000, the adjustment entry will be:
options: Debit C, credit A and B ₹20,000
mcqs.explanation: C gains 2/9 x 90,000 = ₹20,000 and compensates A, who sacrifices the same share.

mcqs.q: A firm has a workmen compensation reserve of ₹60,000. The actual claim is ₹75,000. The excess claim of ₹15,000 is debited to:
options: Partners' capital accounts in new ratio
mcqs.explanation: The excess liability is a loss arising on reassessment of liabilities, so it is debited to the Revaluation Account.

mcqs.q: Investment fluctuation reserve is ₹20,000; investments appear at ₹1,00,000 and their market value is ₹88,000. The amount of IFR credited to partners' capital accounts will be:
mcqs.explanation: ₹12,000 of the reserve is used to write down investments; the balance 20,000 − 12,000 = ₹8,000 goes to partners in old ratio.

mcqs.q:
Assertion (A): Accumulated profits appearing in the balance sheet at the time of change in profit-sharing ratio are distributed in the old ratio.
Reason (R): These profits were earned when the old ratio was in force.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
mcqs.explanation: Since the profits relate to the period of the old agreement, they belong to partners in the old ratio; R explains A.

mcqs.q: Profit or loss on revaluation at the time of change in profit-sharing ratio is shared among partners in:
mcqs.explanation: Changes in values relate to the period before the change, so the old ratio applies.

mcqs.q: Case: P, Q and R share profits equally. They decide to share in the ratio 2:2:1 from 1 April 2025. Goodwill is valued at ₹1,50,000. The amount credited to R's capital account for goodwill will be:
mcqs.explanation: R's sacrifice = 1/3 − 1/5 = 2/15; 2/15 x 1,50,000 = ₹20,000, debited to P and Q ₹10,000 each (each gains 1/15).

mcqs.q:
Assertion (A): When the profit-sharing ratio changes, the gaining partner compensates the sacrificing partner for goodwill.
Reason (R): As per AS-26, goodwill is raised in the books at its full value and retained as an asset.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
mcqs.explanation: A is true. R is false: AS-26 does not allow self-generated goodwill to be raised; that is why it is adjusted through capital accounts.

mcqs.q: Goodwill already appearing in the balance sheet at the time of change in profit-sharing ratio is written off among partners in:
mcqs.explanation: Existing goodwill belongs to the old arrangement and is written off in the old ratio before the new goodwill adjustment.

mcqs.q: X and Y share profits equally and decide to share 2:1 in future. A general reserve of ₹60,000 is to remain in the books. The adjustment entry is:
mcqs.explanation: X gains 2/3 − 1/2 = 1/6; Y sacrifices 1/6. 60,000 x 1/6 = ₹10,000: X debited, Y credited.

mcqs.q: An increase in the value of a liability on revaluation is:
options: Credited directly to partners' capital accounts
Debited to Profit and Loss A/c
mcqs.explanation: A higher liability means a loss to the partners, so it is debited to the Revaluation Account.

questions.q: State the formula for calculating gaining ratio.
questions.answerHtml: Gaining ratio = New ratio − Old ratio (for each gaining partner).

questions.q: In which ratio is a general reserve distributed among partners at the time of a change in profit-sharing ratio?
questions.answerHtml: In the old profit-sharing ratio, because it was built up out of profits earned under the old ratio.
